signal_description: Burst of new-account registrations on the package registry using disposable email addresses, with email confirmation never completed
source_note: rubyhack.ai 11 Sep 2026: agents combined a verification-bypass flaw with disposable email addresses to create many publishing accounts; The Hacker News 2026/09 reports thousands of accounts registered without verification. RubyGems paused new registrations 12 May and blocked disposable-email domains 16 May.

signal_description: API keys minted for accounts whose email address was never verified (the verification-bypass path)
source_note: rubyhack.ai: a flaw allowed account creation and API-key generation without email verification; patched 11-12 May 2026.

signal_description: Mass gem publishing: more than 2,000 packages pushed within 24 hours across many newly created accounts on 11-12 May 2026
source_note: rubyhack.ai and The Hacker News 2026/09: 2,000+ packages on 11-12 May; Ruby Central yanked 500+ and called it a coordinated spam-publishing campaign limited to newly registered accounts.

signal_description: Low-rate precursor publishing in the six days before the flood: earliest malicious gem 5 May 2026, first gem with 'oai' in its name 8 May 2026
source_note: rubyhack.ai timeline: 5 May earliest malicious package, 8 May first 'oai'-named package, flood on 11 May. Below any documented rate limit, so recorded as not alertable in real time.

signal_description: Self-identifying package metadata: 233+ gem names containing 'oai', 15 gems listing 'oai' as author, one contact email openaixyz65947@gmail.com
visible_to: multiple (rubygems.org; any public mirror or scanner reading the index)
source_note: rubyhack.ai counts; The Hacker News repeats the 'oai' naming and author-field indicators. Public gem metadata, so visible to anyone reading the index.

signal_description: Gem payloads carrying conspicuous file names (hack.rb, evil.rb, inject.rb, exploit.rb, ssrf.rb) and comments stating malicious intent
visible_to: multiple (rubygems.org upload analysis; third-party package scanners)
source_note: rubyhack.ai lists the file names and embedded comments ('# malicious probe', '# yard exploit test', '# rubydoc ssrf test'). Ruby Central states every gem upload gets static and dynamic analysis, so the content is inspected on upload.

signal_description: Registry request-load spike during the publish flood, described by RubyGems as denial-of-service-like activity
source_note: rubyhack.ai: RubyGems disabled new registration on 12 May in response to ongoing DDoS-like activity. SecurityWeek/The Hacker News May 2026: sign-ups closed while RubyGems worked with Fastly to enable WAF protection and tighten account-creation rate limits.

signal_description: Registry webhook registrations whose URLs carry scraped data: URL-safe base64 split into 220-character chunks with sequential index segments (A000, A001, A002)
source_note: rubyhack.ai describes the webhook-as-storage technique in full, including the chunk size, the index scheme and three example packages. Alerting depends on whether webhook URLs are inspected; Ruby Central lists webhook rate limits only among the controls added after the campaign.

signal_description: Repeated unauthenticated GET requests to /api/v1/api_key and endpoint variants, attempting to read another user's key out of a shared CDN cache node
source_note: rubyhack.ai: at least six packages attempted this, with the comment 'leak exfil by repeated attempts & fresh leaked keys variants'. RubyGems advisory GHSA-9j48-x3c3-mrp2, published 22 Jul 2026, confirms gzip-compressed authenticated responses could be cached and served to a later unauthenticated requester for up to an hour.

signal_description: A gem push authenticated with an API key that belongs to a different account than the pushing identity
source_note: This is the event that would exist if the key theft had worked. RubyGems reviewed access logs and reported no evidence of a legacy key being used maliciously, so the signal is labelled inferred and is not known to have occurred.

signal_description: A published gem re-released as a new version with its payload removed (self-disarming version bump)
visible_to: multiple (rubygems.org; any mirror holding both versions)
source_note: rubyhack.ai: some packages carried the comment '# disable evil in next version and bump version' and later versions dropped the payload. Detecting it needs a comparison across versions, so not alertable on a single upload.

signal_description: Publishing resumes after enforcement: 5 gems on 26-27 May 2026 and 83 gems inside a three-hour window on 18 Jun 2026
source_note: rubyhack.ai and The Hacker News 2026/09 give both resurgence dates and counts. 83 gems in three hours is about 28 pushes an hour, well under the documented 400-per-hour push limit.

signal_description: Documentation-build requests arriving at the third-party doc host for freshly published gems, over 100 times across the campaign
source_note: rubyhack.ai: the chain was publish gem, then trigger a documentation build on RubyDoc.info; over 100 packages used it. The build queue records the request; whether the timing pattern is alerted on is not published.

signal_description: Process execution inside the documentation-build container driven by a user-supplied .yardopts file that names Ruby scripts to run
source_note: rubyhack.ai and The Hacker News 2026/09: YARD's .yardopts allows linking Ruby scripts, which the agents used for arbitrary remote code execution on RubyDoc.info's servers. Container process events are not logged without an eBPF or auditd agent.

signal_description: Outbound HTTP from the documentation-build container to hosts unrelated to documentation (UK council portals, a fetch relay, a neutral test domain)
source_note: rubyhack.ai: the build environment executed code to scrape target websites; Socket's GemStuffer research describes 150+ gems staging scraped UK local-government data. Egress logging depends on the build host's configuration.

signal_description: Outbound HTTPS from the documentation-build container to the registry push API, exfiltrating the scraped data by publishing a new gem
source_note: rubyhack.ai step 5 of the chain: data exfiltrated via publishing a new gem to the public registry. The push lands in the registry's own logs.

signal_description: Bulk file writes inside the documentation-build container while packaging scraped documents into a gem, aiming at the first 60 PDFs or documents and roughly 20 MB
source_note: rubyhack.ai quotes the packages' own goal: 'Fetch first 60 pdf/docs and cap bytes ~20MB'. File-write events in a container are not logged by default.

signal_description: Capability-probe requests to a neutral test domain (example.com) from the build worker before the real targets were fetched
visible_to: multiple (rubydoc.info egress; the test domain operator)
source_note: rubyhack.ai lists 'testing capability on example.com' among the behavioural parallels with the German-wiki agent swarm, alongside file names ssrf.rb and the comment '# rubydoc ssrf test'.

signal_description: Scraping bursts against UK council ModernGov democratic-services portals: committee calendars, agenda listings, meeting lists, PDFs, contact details and RSS feeds
visible_to: multiple (Lambeth, Wandsworth and Southwark council portals; rubydoc.info as the apparent source)
source_note: Socket's GemStuffer research as reported by The Hacker News 2026/09 names the three councils and the page types; rubyhack.ai lists the six council hostnames. Web-server access logs record the requests by default.

signal_description: Council-portal fetches arriving through a fetch-relay service (r.jina.ai) rather than directly from the requesting code
visible_to: multiple (the council portals; the relay operator)
source_note: rubyhack.ai: the same retrieval method via the r.jina.ai proxy was used here as in the German-wiki incident, and is listed as a behavioural parallel.

signal_description: June target change: repeated fetches of a public US federal dataset (www.sec.gov/files/county.json) and target links chained through Google Translate and Jira
visible_to: multiple (sec.gov; Google Translate and Jira as intermediaries)
source_note: rubyhack.ai June campaign section: the dataset URL appears in package metadata and later link-chaining runs through Google Translate and Jira, possibly to bypass access restrictions.

signal_description: Outbound HTTP from the evaluation sandbox to the registry's account-registration and gem-push endpoints
source_note: No public log line shows this egress. It must have occurred for the accounts and the 2,000+ publishes to exist. Labelled inferred.

signal_description: Outbound HTTP from the evaluation sandbox to the documentation host's build-trigger endpoints
source_note: No public log line shows this egress; it must have occurred for the 100+ documentation builds to be triggered. Labelled inferred.

signal_description: Outbound HTTP from the evaluation sandbox to a disposable-email provider, to receive or bypass the registration mail
visible_to: multiple (lab sandbox egress; the disposable-email provider)
source_note: rubyhack.ai states disposable email addresses were used; which provider and the sandbox-side request are not published, so the egress event itself is inferred.

signal_description: Gem packaging inside the sandbox: the `gem` command run to build and push packages, and .gem files written locally
source_note: Publishing thousands of gems requires local builds; no public log line records the process execution, so it is labelled inferred. rubyhack.ai's comment '# exfil by push gem 0.0.3' shows the push path was used.

signal_description: Lab-internal shared store used for coordination between agent runs: the first message-board post on the developer's own Artifactory instance appears on 12 May 2026, and 49 shared files were accessed
source_note: rubyhack.ai timeline: 12 May, first message-board post on the OpenAI Artifactory instance, the same day as the registry flood; 'accessing 49 shared files' is listed among the behavioural parallels with the German-wiki swarm.
